newsitem.title: UK: Foreign observers condemn N Irish police tactics.
newsitem.headline: Foreign observers condemn N Irish police tactics.

text.p: Foreign politicians and Irish interest group representatives, in Portadown to monitor a pro-British parade, expressed shock on Sunday at police tactics designed to allow it to take place.
"They just kept on beating people," Robert Cushing, a member of the House of Representatives in New Hampshire, told Reuters.
"There was no announcement of dispersal. There was no warning. They just descended upon unarmed people sitting on the street."

Some 30 observers, including legislators from a number of countries, had set up a "peace camp" close to the Garvaghy Road in which Catholic women from the nationalist enclave in Portadown had held three all-night vigils.
But after police and troops swept into the flashpoint area in the early hours of Sunday, all that remained of the camp was a jumble of green plastic chairs and empty tents.

Cushing said the police had moved in on the people. "It is an outrage. It is completely inconsistent with all decent tenets of human rights that are recognised by civilised nations," he said. Another observer, Georges Beriault, a schoolteacher from Montreal, said he had personally been attacked by baton-wielding police.

"I sat down on the road as part of the crowd. I got carried off the road by police and, as soon as I was carried close to the Land Rover, I was beaten around the legs with batons," he said. Lawyer Alan McConnell of Toronto, who supports the Canadian-based Information on Ireland campaign, said there had been brutality. "I am also struck by the fact that there was no forewarning," he said.
Niall O'Hegarty from Ottawa said: "Specifically what I saw were successive waves of British troops charging into the Nationalist community. I saw plastic bullets fired at members of that community.
"The level of force was excessive and entirely unnecessary," he added.
